govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BarceloJohnJJr_: nsia-BarceloJohnJJr Barcelo John J Jr: the declassified government document on John Barcelo Jr, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, preserved as released. An obscure item, of the files. From the archive's collection, for researchers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ConnallyJohnBJr:
On April 21, 1964, Governor John B. Connally and his wife testified before the Warren Commission about the day President Kennedy was killed in Dallas. Connally had been riding in the president's car and was badly wounded himself. Research notes preserved here work through what the couple told the commission.

The notes focus on two points in their account: how many shots the Connallys heard, and how the governor's injuries happened. Both points matter because Connally's memory of the shooting was key evidence for the commission's version of events. The notes let readers follow that testimony point by point.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HowardLawrenceJ:
A letter dated June 9, 1968, addressed to Jim, discusses an interrogation held on February 25. The man questioned was named Howard. The writer also covers Jerry Cohen's confirmation of points in the matter and possible Frente-Varona activity in New Orleans, a Cuban exile political current in the city.

Letters like this one passed intelligence hand to hand inside the investigation world. An interrogation, a confirmation, and exile activity are weighed in a few pages between men working the same case. The writer is unnamed in the record, but the contents show the New Orleans exile angle still alive in 1968.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LandisPaulEJr_L:
Paul E. Landis Jr. was a Secret Service agent on duty in Dallas when President Kennedy was killed. His official statement describes his activities and duties on November 22, 1963. It begins with his arrival at Love Field with the presidential party. It then follows him through the motorcade across the city.

Statements like this one were the basic building blocks of the official record. Each agent wrote down where he stood, what he did, and what he saw. Landis's account lets readers trace the protection detail's movements that day in the plain language of a report written for the file, close to the events it describes.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LauchliRichardJ:
John R. Harpster reported this story for the Decatur Herald in May 1964. Federal agents had posed as foreign buyers in an undercover operation. Two men were arrested, among them Richard Lauchli Jr., a regional leader of the Minutemen. The Minutemen were a paramilitary group whose members stockpiled weapons against a feared communist takeover.

The arrests show one way federal agents worked such groups in the early 1960s: a staged purchase rather than a raid. Lauchli's name also appears in assassination research, because the Minutemen and their gun networks drew official attention after Dallas. The article is a hometown paper's account of the sting and the men it caught.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-McCloskeyPaulJr:
Congressman Paul N. McCloskey Jr. of California wrote this letter, dated April 10, to Harold Weisberg. Weisberg's address was his own small press, Coq d'Or Press. McCloskey represented California's 17th District. In the letter he offered Weisberg his personal help in obtaining information.

Members of Congress could open doors that stayed shut to private citizens, by writing agencies on a constituent's or a writer's behalf. Weisberg spent years seeking assassination records, and letters like this one were tools of that search. The letter preserves an offer of help from a sitting congressman. It does not show what information, if any, the offer produced.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TellRoyJr_Tell_: FBI agents interviewed Roy Tell Jr. on December 2, 1963, about Lee Harvey Oswald and the Civil Air Patrol. Tell said Oswald's name was vaguely familiar to him. The Civil Air Patrol mattered because Oswald had joined it as a teenager in New Orleans. The interview shows agents testing even faint memories for a link between Oswald and the people around that youth program.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WaltonAlbertJr_: Harold Weisberg wrote to Mr. Walton on July 28, 1970, declining extensive correspondence. Weisberg received more mail than one man could answer, and he sometimes had to say so plainly. The letter is short evidence of that burden. It also shows his direct manner: a researcher guarding his time for the files and books he thought mattered most.
henry-james-jr: William Dean Howells's critical appreciation of his friend Henry James, written when James was still a young writer. Howells praises the precision and psychological depth of the early novels and stories, defending the new realism against old-fashioned romance. A fascinating document of two giants of American literature sizing each other up in the 1880s.
the-rubaiyat-of-omar-khayyam-jr:
Wallace Irwin presents The Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám Jr. as a translation from the original Bornese into English verse, with eight illustrations and a cover design by Gelett Burgess. Its introduction is a comic performance that treats the whole book as a newly unearthed sensation in the world of letters.

The editor argues that since Fitzgerald's 1851 translation, imitators had stretched the one Omar too thin, so the true need was for more Omars to translate. He claims the superior later Omar lay undiscovered in the wilds of Borneo, written in an ancient Mango-Bornese dialect burdened with thousands of irregular verbs. The joke frames the quatrains that follow as a deliberate parody.
